Laurel/Team — putting numbers and a succinct ops-level plan below. I am keeping language conservative (SLO vs SLA) except where we have dedicated reserved contracts.

On Tue, Aug 18, 2026 at 10:03 AM laura.bennett@redwood.com wrote:
> Karthik / Marissa — forwarding EverGuard's follow-up. They want a concise DR runbook + explicit RTO/RPO numbers for hosted and dedicated.

Draft answers (feel free to trim):

1) RTO / RPO (typical operating assumptions)
- Hosted API (multi-tenant): RTO target: 15 minutes for automated routing & fallback to alternate region; conservative end-to-end recovery window for full traffic restoration: 30-60 minutes depending on model load. RPO: near-zero for control-plane metadata; for in-flight token streams we do not persist ephemeral KV/state — we recommend application-level checkpointing for long-running interactive sessions.
- Dedicated Reserved Pools (customer-dedicated): RTO target: 10 minutes for routing to warm standby region (if warm standby enabled). If cold failover/restore of model artifacts is required, end-to-end recovery: 60-120 minutes (model load + cache warm-up). RPO: near-zero for committed artifacts and stored datasets; application session state depends on customer config (we support prefix caching for common prompts).
- Private/VPC (on-prem) deployments: RTO/RPO are driven by customer infra; we provide failover playbooks and tooling; typical guidance: RTO 60-180 minutes for cold restores, RPO configurable via customer replication.

2) Multi-region failover runbook (high-level sequence)
- Detection: Monitoring alerts (region-wide health checks) route to SRE + on-call. Automated health probes detect region unavailability.
- Automated routing: For hosted API customers, traffic is automatically routed to the next healthy region per routing policy (takes ~2-15 minutes depending on DNS & CDN TTL).
- Model variant fallback: If the preferred model is unavailable, requests route to compatible variant (quantized smaller model) to maintain availability.
- Warm standby: For Dedicated pools with warm standby enabled, we keep model artifacts in standby region and KV caches pre-warmed for top-N models; cutover includes reassigning pool endpoints and triggering canary traffic validation (validation window 5-10 minutes).
- Manual escalation: If automated routing does not restore service, SRE executes the manual playbook: promote standby pool, reconfigure network endpoints, validate key traffic paths, and notify account team + customer-facing CS.
- Post-mortem & rollback: After restoration, we run validation tests, collect logs, and coordinate any necessary rollbacks or follow-ups.

3) Constraints affecting recovery time
- Model load time: Large model cold-starts ( >70B parameters) can take 20–80 minutes to load depending on quantization and hardware. Quantized variants reduce load times to 5–20 minutes.
- KV cache warm-up: Cache effectiveness improves over minutes-to-hours; we save popular prefixes where possible but cold caches increase early latency.
- Data residency: Customers in strict residency zones may require region pinning; cross-region failover may be restricted by policy/contract.

Attachments to include: short runbook doc and an architecture diagram. I recommend we state RTO targets as "operational targets" and reserve SLA commitments to dedicated contracts (we can commit SLA credits under reserved capacity agreements).

Let me know if you want these condensed to bullet points for the customer doc.

— Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference

David — thanks for the ask and for the timeline. Answers and materials below (attached docs: Redwood_DR_Summary_v1.pdf, regional-failover-runbook.docx, runbook-diagram.png). We kept things concise to make it RFP-friendly.

Good-faith summary (customer-ready):
- Hosted API (multi-tenant): operational RTO target: 15 minutes for automated routing to an alternate region; realistic full recovery and model load window of 30–60 minutes for large models. RPO: near-zero for control plane metadata; ephemeral session state should be handled by the application.
- Dedicated Reserved Pools: operational RTO target: 10 minutes with warm standby enabled; cold restores may require 60–120 minutes depending on model size and quantization. RPO: near-zero for persisted artifacts; application session state configurable.
- Private/VPC deployments: RTO/RPO depend on customer topology; we provide a playbook and guidance for reduceable RTOs with warm replication.

Runbook highlights (high-level):
1) Automated detection & routing: health probes trigger routing policy to shift traffic within ~2–15 minutes (DNS + CDN TTL dependent).
2) Validation canary: we run small canary traffic for 5–10 minutes to validate model responses and latency post-cutover.
3) Manual escalation: SRE elevates to full manual failover if automation doesn’t restore service; responsible teams: SRE (lead), Infrastructure (model restore), CS (customer comms).
4) Post-incident steps: post-mortem, user-impact mapping, and regression tests tied to our Optimize pipeline.

Important constraints and recommendations:
- Large-model cold start times are the largest single contributor to extended recovery windows; customers with tight RTOs should enable warm standby or maintain a quantized variant as an always-available fallback.
- If strict data residency prevents cross-region failover, RTO will be influenced by the customer's own DR processes.

We are happy to adapt the runbook language into EverGuard's RFP template or provide a redlined DOCX. If helpful, we can schedule a 30-minute technical walkthrough with our SRE lead to talk through warm-standby options and model warming strategies.
